rules.statement: Present a rotating refresh token to the provider at most once: serialize refreshes of one session locally and, across replicas, admit one refresher through a lease keyed by the session key plus a SHA-256 fingerprint of the refresh token, not by a record version.
rules.why: Presenting a rotated refresh token twice counts as reuse and revokes the whole token family (RFC 9700 §4.14.2). A version-keyed lease is unsafe because unrelated writes bump the version and would let a second refresher in with the same token.
rules.check: Look for refresh-token grant code with no cross-replica single-flight guard, or with a lease/lock keyed by something other than the refresh token's identity (record version, timestamp, etc.).

rules.statement: A refresher that loses the lease must wait for the winner's result by polling with backoff and give up with a 503 at the lease duration; it must never retry with the old refresh token after a timeout or present a token whose lease another replica holds.
rules.why: Retrying with the old token after a timeout is exactly the reuse that revokes the token family.
rules.check: Look for wait/timeout paths in refresh logic that fall back to sending the refresh token they originally read, or that skip taking the lease again after the refresh token changes.

rules.statement: When an optimistic-concurrency write that persists a rotated refresh token loses a version race, merge it onto the newer version and retry; never drop it.
rules.why: If the write is dropped, the only copy of the rotated refresh token is lost, and the next refresh presents the old token, which the provider treats as reuse.
rules.check: Look for read-modify-write of refreshed tokens where a concurrency conflict is ignored, logged and skipped, or overwritten with stale data instead of being merged and retried.

rules.statement: Once a refresh has won the lease, run the token request and the persistence of its result with CancellationToken.None, bounded only by the client's request timeout, not by the caller's cancellation token.
rules.why: If the caller aborts after the provider rotated the token, the session keeps the old refresh token and the next refresh presents it again, which is reuse.
rules.check: Look for the caller's request/HttpContext cancellation token passed to the refresh-token request or to the write-back that stores the rotated token.

rules.statement: A holder of an expiring distributed lease may release it only when it finished with a safety margin before the lease expires, so it never deletes a lease that expired and another node took.
rules.why: Releasing after expiry could delete another replica's live lease and admit a second concurrent holder.
rules.check: Look for unconditional lease/lock release in finally blocks without checking remaining lease time or ownership.

rules.statement: Use a per-key lock that is reference-counted and removed when its last waiter leaves, not striped locks, when a holder may block for a long time.
rules.why: A stripe held while waiting out a long operation blocks every unrelated key hashed to the same stripe.
rules.check: Look for striped/hashed lock arrays guarding operations that can wait on remote leases or I/O, or for per-key lock dictionaries that never remove entries.

rules.statement: Map refresh failures as follows: invalid_grant ends the session and answers 401, any other OAuth error answers 502, and provider exceptions, HttpRequestException or timeouts answer 503. A session that needs a new token but has no refresh token ends with 401.
rules.why: Only invalid_grant means the grant is dead. Other failures are provider or transport problems and must not end the user's session.
rules.check: Look for refresh error handling that ends the session on transient or transport errors, or that collapses every failure into one status code.

rules.statement: Treat a token response without expires_in as already expiring, so the token is refreshed on first use, and refresh a token once it is within the configured margin of its expiry.
rules.why: With no known lifetime, the client cannot assume the token is still valid.
rules.check: Look for code that assumes a default or infinite lifetime when expires_in is missing, or that refreshes only after the token has already expired.

rules.statement: When a token response carries refresh_token_expires_in, cap the session's absolute expiry and the cookie's Max-Age at it. Apply the cap only to shorten, never to extend.
rules.why: The session cannot outlive its refresh token, and a provider value must never lengthen a session past its configured absolute lifetime.
rules.check: Look for code that sets the session expiry directly from refresh_token_expires_in without taking the minimum with the existing expiry.

rules.statement: Pin the DPoP key thumbprint (jkt) reported at the code exchange and pass it on every refresh, so a session keeps its key across key-ring rotation.
rules.why: Refresh tokens and access tokens are bound to one key, and rotating the key ring must not break existing sessions.
rules.check: Look for refresh requests that choose the current key-ring key instead of the session's pinned jkt.

rules.statement: A DPoP resource request must include ath in the proof, record every DPoP-Nonce response header, and retry a use_dpop_nonce challenge only once, buffering the request content before the first send.
rules.why: RFC 9449 §7 and §8 require an access-token hash and server-supplied nonces. A request body that is not buffered cannot be resent, and retrying without limit could loop.
rules.check: Look for DPoP handlers that omit ath, ignore DPoP-Nonce on successful responses, retry more than once, or resend HttpContent that was not buffered.

rules.statement: Validate at startup any option whose safe value depends on another option (such as a lease duration that must cover retried requests under the request timeout), and refuse to start when the combination is unsafe.
rules.why: An option combination that is unsafe causes subtle concurrency failures at runtime, while failing at startup surfaces the misconfiguration right away.
rules.check: Look for new duration or timeout options that depend on other timeouts but have no startup validation of how they relate.

rules.statement: When a name does not resolve to a registered strategy, throw InvalidOperationException because it is a configuration error, and report expected runtime failures through a result type that carries a status and reason.
rules.why: It separates programmer or configuration mistakes from runtime conditions that callers need to handle.
rules.check: Look for lookups by strategy name that return a failure result for unknown names, or that throw exceptions for expected runtime failures.
